cards.front: A {{c1::cladogram}} is a branching diagram of proposed relationships.
cards.quote: A cladogram is a branching diagram of proposed relationships.
cards.section: Explore: build a tree one trait at a time

cards.front: A {{c1::shared derived characteristic}} is a trait that first appeared in one ancestor and passed to its descendants.
cards.quote: a trait that first appeared in one ancestor and passed to its descendants
cards.section: Explain: read and build a cladogram

cards.front: Why can a backbone not split one group of vertebrates into smaller groups on a cladogram?
cards.back: Every animal in the group has it, so it cannot tell any of them apart. It is inherited, but it is not new within the group.
cards.quote: A trait every sampled organism has, like a backbone among vertebrates, is inherited too but cannot split them.
cards.section: Explore: build a tree one trait at a time

cards.front: On a cladogram, a branch point (node) is the {{c1::common ancestor}} of every branch that grows from it.
cards.quote: the common ancestor of every branch that grows from it
cards.section: Explain: read and build a cladogram

cards.front: On a cladogram, is a node a single individual animal? What sits at the tips of the tree?
cards.back: No. A node is an ancestral population that lived in the past. Living species sit at the tips.
cards.quote: a node is an ancestral population that lived in the past, not a single individual; living species sit at the tips.
cards.section: Explain: read and build a cladogram

cards.front: A {{c1::homologous structure}} is a body part built from the same basic parts because it came from a common ancestor.
cards.quote: a homologous structure: a body part built from the same basic parts because it came from a common ancestor.
cards.section: Explain: the evidence for shared ancestry

cards.front: In a trait table, the {{c1::outgroup}} is the animal used for comparison.
cards.quote: is the outgroup, the animal used for comparison.
cards.section: Elaborate: score six animals and place a whale

cards.front: In the tree builder, you add the same traits in a different order. What changes and what stays the same?
cards.back: The steps in the drawing change. The finished tree, and so the relationships it shows, stays the same.
cards.quote: Another order changes the steps, not the finished tree.
cards.section: Explore: build a tree one trait at a time

cards.front: In a six-animal trait table, the lamprey has a backbone but no jaws. Tuna, salamander, turtle and leopard all have both. Which trait separates the lamprey from the other four, and where does the lamprey branch?
cards.back: Jaws separate it. The lamprey branches off before the jaw trait appears.
cards.why: A trait marks the branch only for animals that have it and animals that lack it differ.
cards.quote: it has a backbone but no jaws, so it branches off before the jaw trait.
cards.section: Elaborate: score six animals and place a whale

cards.front: Turtle, salamander and leopard all have a backbone, jaws and four walking legs. Only the turtle and leopard have an amnion. Which two are closer relatives, and why do the other three traits not decide?
cards.back: Turtle and leopard. They share the amnion, so their paths meet at a more recent branch point. The other traits are shared by all three, so they cannot pick out a closer pair.
cards.quote: Legs, jaws and a backbone are shared by all three, so they cannot decide.
cards.section: Elaborate: score six animals and place a whale

cards.front: A backbone occurs in every vertebrate in a sample. Can it separate the turtle from the salamander and the leopard in that sample? What kind of trait is needed instead?
cards.back: No. A later trait, such as the amnion, is needed.
cards.why: A trait present in every member of a group cannot divide that group.
cards.quote: A trait shared by every organism in the group cannot split that group.
cards.section: Explain: the evidence for shared ancestry

cards.front: Early fish, chick and human embryos all have a tail and pharyngeal arches. In fish, the arches help form gills. What do they become in humans?
cards.back: Parts of the jaw, ear and throat. The grooves between the arches never open into gill slits, and the tail shrinks.
cards.quote: The arches form parts of the jaw, ear and throat, and the tail shrinks.
cards.section: Explain: the evidence for shared ancestry

cards.front: Why do the tail and pharyngeal arches in early fish, chick and human embryos count as evidence of shared ancestry?
cards.back: They are inherited structures found in several vertebrate groups. They are best explained by a common ancestor whose embryos had them. They do not mean a human embryo turns into a fish.
cards.quote: Early fish, chick and human embryos have a tail and neck folds called pharyngeal arches.
cards.section: Explain: the evidence for shared ancestry

cards.front: The {{c1::fossil record}} is the collection of preserved remains and traces of past life, placed in time order by the rock layers they are found in.
cards.quote: placed in time order by the rock layers they are found in, including groups that no longer exist.
cards.section: Explain: the evidence for shared ancestry

cards.front: Two species have DNA or protein sequences that match closely. What does that suggest about when they shared an ancestor?
cards.back: They usually shared an ancestor more recently. The more the sequences match, the more recent the shared ancestor.
cards.quote: The more two species' sequences match, the more recently they usually shared an ancestor.
cards.section: Explain: the evidence for shared ancestry

cards.front: Almost every organism reads DNA with the same genetic code and shares basic reactions for breaking down sugar. What explains this best?
cards.back: Common ancestry. A shared code and shared chemistry point to a common origin for life, while smaller differences help resolve later branches.
cards.quote: A shared code and shared chemistry are best explained by common ancestry.
cards.section: Explain: the evidence for shared ancestry

cards.front: Mitochondria read a few DNA words differently from the standard genetic code. Does this overturn the idea that the code is nearly universal?
cards.back: No. These are small changes to the same code, so the code is still nearly universal and still points to a common origin.
cards.quote: Some organisms and mitochondria read a few of these words differently, but these are small changes to the same code.
cards.section: Explain: the evidence for shared ancestry

cards.front: A student reads a cladogram and says humans and chimpanzees share a node, so humans came from chimpanzees. Using the tree-reading rule, what is wrong?
cards.back: Both species sit at tips. Tracing back, their paths meet at a node, which is an ancestral population that lived in the past. Each living species descends from that ancestor, not one from the other.
cards.quote: Put a finger on each tip, trace toward the root and stop at the first branch point both paths share.
cards.section: Explain: read and build a cladogram

cards.front: A whale and a tuna are both streamlined swimmers with fins. What kind of evidence should decide where the whale belongs on the tree?
cards.back: Inherited traits that mark a branch, such as lungs and milk, not a resemblance in shape. Lungs separate the whale from the tuna, and milk places it among mammals.
cards.quote: each piece of evidence should be an inherited trait that marks a branch, not a resemblance.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: One DNA spot groups whale with pig, but several other spots group whale with hippo. Should the one spot decide the tree?
cards.back: No. One odd result could reflect missing data or another problem. It should not outweigh several checked, independent insertions.
cards.quote: One odd result could reflect missing data or another problem, so it should not outweigh several checked, independent insertions
cards.section: Elaborate: score six animals and place a whale

cards.front: In 2005 a team compared one chimpanzee genome with human DNA. Across the aligned parts they found 1.23 mismatches per 100 bases. About how many of every 1,000 aligned bases differ?
cards.back: 1.23 x 10 = 12.3 per 1,000, so about 12 bases differ.
cards.quote: they found 1.23 mismatches per 100 bases, so about 98.8 percent matched.
cards.section: The 2005 chimpanzee genome comparison

cards.front: The human and chimpanzee comparison found about 98.8 percent of bases matched. What does that figure cover and what does it leave out?
cards.back: It covers only the parts of the genomes that could be lined up. It does not include every difference between the two genomes.
cards.quote: That figure covers only the aligned parts, not every difference between the two genomes.
cards.section: The 2005 chimpanzee genome comparison

cards.front: Plan a study to test whether whales are closer to hippos or to pigs using inserted pieces of DNA. What do you measure, and what result supports each answer?
cards.back: Measure, at many matching DNA spots, whether an insertion is present or absent in whale, hippo, pig, cow and an outgroup such as a horse. Several insertions shared by whale and hippo but not pig support whale with hippo. Several shared by hippo and pig but not whale support hippo with pig. Rests on the rule that shared derived traits mark closest relatives.
cards.quote: at many matching DNA spots, whether an inserted piece of DNA is present or absent in whales, hippos, pigs, cows and an outgroup such as a horse
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the insertion study of whales, hippos and pigs, why test many DNA spots and more than one individual of each species?
cards.back: So that a single odd result cannot decide the answer. Several independent spots agreeing is stronger evidence than one.
cards.quote: use many spots, not one, so that a single odd result cannot decide the answer.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A new animal is scored 1 for backbone, jaws, four walking legs and amnion, and 0 for hair. In the six-animal table the 1s nest. Where does it branch, and which traits place it?
cards.back: Its scores match the turtle exactly, so the table cannot tell them apart: it falls with the turtle in the amnion group, below the leopard's hair branch. The amnion places it there and the missing hair keeps it off the leopard branch. Rests on the rule that the 1s nest, with each trait marking a smaller group.
cards.quote: The 1s nest: five animals have backbones, four have jaws, three have four walking legs, two have an amnion and one has hair.
cards.section: Elaborate: score six animals and place a whale

cards.front: Dolphin embryos grow hind-limb buds that stop growing around week five. A student says this is only a resemblance. Using the lesson's evidence rule, how do you defend the buds as evidence for where whales belong?
cards.back: The buds are an inherited embryo trait, not just a look-alike shape. Together with lungs, milk and, in the lesson's made-up DNA example, insertions shared with hippos, they are several lines of evidence from inherited traits pointing to mammals. Rests on the rule that evidence must be inherited traits that mark a branch.
cards.quote: Dolphin embryos grow hind-limb buds that stop growing around week five.
cards.section: Dates for the whale evidence

cards.front: Name the ranks of classification in order from broadest to most specific.
cards.back: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
cards.quote: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
cards.section: Classification ranks and embryo drawings

cards.front: Some old textbook drawings made vertebrate embryos look more alike than they really are. What do biologists use now, and what do the shared structures still show?
cards.back: They compare photographs of real embryos. The shared structures are evidence, but the embryos are not identical.
cards.quote: The shared structures are evidence; the embryos are not identical.
cards.section: Classification ranks and embryo drawings

cards.front: What does a cladogram say about an organism that was not included in the sample it was built from?
cards.back: Nothing. A tree is a supported model of the organisms and evidence it includes, and new evidence can test it.
cards.quote: It says nothing about organisms left out, and new evidence can test it.
cards.section: Explore: build a tree one trait at a time
